transcript:
Fireflies.ai - Transcript

Title: Security review: Dedicated Burst beta (isolation, audit logs, data residency)
Date: 2025-07-10 10:00 AM PT
Duration: 47 min

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Markus Klein, Marcus Lin, Kaitlyn Nguyen, Ethan Park
Northpeak Financial: Ariana Patel (Security Architect), Jonas Meyer (GRC), Mikhail Orlov (Platform Eng), Sofia Reyes (Procurement)

Summary (auto-generated)
- Northpeak asked how “Burst” for Dedicated works without breaking tenant isolation.
- Discussed audit logging for burst enablement and limit changes, including who/what/when and export paths.
- Clarified data residency: burst pools are region-scoped; default is same-region-only bursting.
- Reviewed risk posture: strict admission control vs preemption; no guarantee of eviction order; customer can set hard caps and disable burst.

Topics
- Isolation boundaries (compute, network, logging)
- Burst pool sharing model and noisy-neighbor protections
- Audit logs for config changes and policy decisions
- Data residency / region pinning and failover behavior
- Beta terms (shadow metering) and operational controls

Questions (auto-generated)
- Can a burst request ever execute in a different region than the Dedicated tenant’s primary region?
- Are GPUs time-sliced across tenants in burst pools?
- What audit events are emitted when burst is enabled/disabled or limits change?
- Can audit logs be exported to our SIEM?

---

[00:00] Markus Klein: Alright, we’re at the hour. Thanks everyone for joining. This is the security review focused on the Dedicated burst beta. Ariana, Jonas, Mikhail, Sofia — good to meet you all. On our side I’ve got Marcus from security, Kaitlyn who owns authz and isolation, and Ethan who leads the control plane bits.

[00:20] Ariana Patel: Thanks Markus. Yeah, we’re trying to understand whether “burst” basically means we’re moving onto shared infrastructure. And if yes, what exactly is the isolation story.

[00:31] Markus Klein: Totally. Maybe quick framing: your baseline Dedicated is still dedicated capacity. Burst is an opt-in overflow path, with strict admission control. It’s not like we permanently move you to shared. It’s more, under a spike, we can temporarily route some traffic to a controlled shared burst pool.

[00:48] Mikhail Orlov: When you say “route,” is that like request-level routing? Or you spin up more dedicated nodes for us?

[00:56] Ethan Park: Request-level routing. There’s a policy check on each request when baseline is saturated. If it’s eligible and within your configured caps, we’ll admit it to a burst pool in the same region and same GPU class, basically.

[01:12] Ariana Patel: Okay, so then: isolation. Is that shared GPUs, shared processes? Like multi-tenant on the same GPU at the same time?

[01:23] Kaitlyn Nguyen: It’s multi-tenant at the pool level, not within a single inference process. Each request executes in a tenant-scoped workload. We don’t do “two customers in the same model server process” for burst. And we don’t time-slice a single GPU between tenants inside one process.

[01:40] Ariana Patel: But physically it’s the same Kubernetes cluster?

[01:44] Kaitlyn Nguyen: Depends on region. In the beta design, burst pools are separate node groups with their own scheduling labels and network policies. In some regions they’re in the same underlying cluster as the hosted fleet, but with hard scheduling and network segregation. In other regions we deploy as a distinct cluster. Either way, the isolation controls are the same: tenant identity gets propagated and enforced at the control plane and data plane.

[02:07] Jonas Meyer: Sorry, “tenant identity propagated” — can you unpack what that means for logs and audit?

[02:13] Ethan Park: Yeah. Every request has a tenant claim in the auth context, and the burst admission decision is logged with that tenant, the pool, and the decision reason. Then we also write audit events when a human changes burst settings.

[02:28] Sofia Reyes: Before audit logs, I want to be clear: are we leaving our Dedicated environment from a contractual standpoint? Like, would this be “shared” and break some of our internal policy?

[02:40] Markus Klein: It’s still your Dedicated tenant. But yes, when you burst, the compute is drawn from a shared pool. That’s why it’s an add-on with explicit terms. The key is: we treat burst pools as controlled shared capacity with strong tenant separation and no data persistence. And you can set hard guardrails that ensure you never exceed what you’re comfortable with.

[03:02] Ariana Patel: Let’s drill into “no data persistence.” Are prompts/outputs stored anywhere? We have restrictions on retaining PII.

[03:10] Marcus Lin: For inference, prompts and outputs are processed in memory. We don’t train on customer data. Logs are configurable; for Dedicated we can disable payload logging. For burst, same — we don’t turn on payload logging just because it’s burst. The default is metadata and metrics, not content.

[03:31] Ariana Patel: Metrics sometimes include tokens, right? That can still leak.

[03:36] Marcus Lin: Token counts, latency, error codes, admission allow/deny reasons — yes. Not token text. We can share the metric dimensions we emit; we’ve been careful about cardinality and content.

[03:52] Mikhail Orlov: Is there any caching that could cross tenants? Like KV cache reused?

[03:58] Kaitlyn Nguyen: Good question. KV caching is per-request or per-session depending on how you use streaming; any prefix caching we do is scoped to a tenant boundary. We don’t share caches across tenants. The cache keys include tenant context.

[04:16] Ariana Patel: You said “tenant boundary,” is that enforced in code or is it best effort?

[04:21] Kaitlyn Nguyen: Enforced. There’s an authorization layer and the cache namespace uses tenant ID. Also, the routing layer won’t ever intentionally attach you to another tenant’s runtime.

[04:35] Jonas Meyer: What about the scenario where two tenants share the same underlying node and there’s memory leakage risk via GPU memory?

[04:43] Marcus Lin: We do not co-locate two tenants in the same model server process. GPU memory is allocated to a single process/worker. The container runtime boundaries apply. We also clear allocations on teardown. Is it the same as bare metal dedicated physical isolation? No. But it’s consistent with multi-tenant cloud controls. If you need strict single-tenant physical isolation at all times, then you’d keep burst disabled.

[05:11] Ariana Patel: Right, we just need to document the risk. Another angle: data residency. If we’re pinned to, say, us-east, does burst ever go to us-west because it has more headroom?

[05:23] Ethan Park: Default is no. Burst pools are region-scoped and we only admit to pools in your configured region. There’s a separate concept of cross-region failover, but that’s an explicit opt-in and would be documented. For beta, we’re strongly recommending same-region only.

[05:44] Mikhail Orlov: Is it same availability zone? Like, does it stay in the same AZ?

[05:50] Ethan Park: It can be different AZ within the same region because the pool may be spread across AZs. That’s pretty typical. Latency stays in region.

[06:01] Ariana Patel: Okay. Do you have a list of regions where burst pools exist and what cloud provider?

[06:08] Markus Klein: Yes. We can share a one-pager: region, GPU type, and whether it’s AWS or GCP. For Northpeak, we’d propose starting in us-east-1, H100 class.

[06:22] Jonas Meyer: And if we’re under a residency obligation that data must not leave AWS, do you ever burst to GCP?

[06:29] Ethan Park: No, not unless you had multi-cloud enabled and requested it. We can pin you to a cloud + region.

[06:38] Ariana Patel: Good. Next: audit logs. We require audit logs for admin actions — turning burst on/off, changing limits, changing allow-lists. What do you have?

[06:49] Ethan Park: There are two categories. One is configuration change events: who changed what, when, and from what value to what value. The second is policy decision logs — why a request was admitted or denied — but those are more operational logs than compliance audit.

[07:09] Jonas Meyer: Let’s stay on configuration audit. What fields are included?

[07:14] Ethan Park: Actor identity (user/service), auth method, tenant ID, environment, request ID, timestamp, and the diff-like summary: e.g. burst_enabled false -> true, max_burst_tps 2k -> 3k, cooldown 60s -> 120s. Also we log the UI/API client and IP for human actions.

[07:39] Ariana Patel: Is that in the same audit log stream you use for other Dedicated changes?

[07:44] Ethan Park: Yes, same audit log pipeline. Burst adds a few new event types.

[07:52] Mikhail Orlov: Can we receive those in our SIEM? Splunk or Sentinel.

[07:58] Marcus Lin: We support export via webhook and via cloud storage delivery depending on deployment mode. For Dedicated, most customers do webhook to their SIEM collector. We can follow up with the exact formats.

[08:15] Sofia Reyes: Is that an extra cost item?

[08:18] Markus Klein: For beta, we’re not charging extra for audit export. Long-term, extended retention or specialized exports might be in an enterprise tier, but we’re not gating beta on that.

[08:33] Ariana Patel: Okay. Another question: who at Redwood can change our burst limits? We need least privilege.

[08:40] Kaitlyn Nguyen: RBAC in the console: you can restrict who in your org can change burst settings. On Redwood side, our access is controlled; changes by Redwood operators are audited and require break-glass workflows. Also you can require approvals on your side if you use SCIM/SSO groups.

[09:02] Jonas Meyer: Do you support SAML? Sorry, I know this might be in your standard security doc.

[09:06] Markus Klein: Yes, SSO/SAML for console access is supported for Dedicated enterprise. We’ll attach it in the packet.

[09:15] Ariana Patel: Noisy neighbor protections: if burst pool is shared, how do you guarantee we don’t get impacted by another tenant’s spike, and also we don’t impact others?

[09:26] Ethan Park: We do admission control with hard caps. There’s per-tenant concurrency and tokens-per-second caps, and pool-wide saturation gates. Also cooldowns if a tenant trips limits. If the pool is saturated, we deny burst admissions rather than preempting others.

[09:47] Ariana Patel: Deny means what HTTP code?

[09:51] Ethan Park: It can be 429 or 503 depending on why. If you exceeded your configured burst cap, it’s 429 with a reason code. If the pool is saturated, typically 503. There are headers indicating the reason, but they don’t leak internal topology.

[10:11] Mikhail Orlov: And if burst is denied, do you fall back to baseline or to another model?

[10:16] Ethan Park: Baseline is always the first attempt. If baseline is saturated and burst denied, you either get denied or you can configure fallback (like a smaller model) but that’s an explicit routing policy.

[10:32] Ariana Patel: From a compliance standpoint, fallback to another model is still within our tenant, right?

[10:37] Kaitlyn Nguyen: Correct, still within your tenant context. Model choice doesn’t change tenant isolation.

[10:44] Jonas Meyer: Do you emit audit log events for policy decisions? Like “request denied due to pool saturation.”

[10:51] Ethan Park: Not as compliance audit, but we log it in operational logs and metrics. We can provide those metrics in the console and via API.

[11:02] Ariana Patel: Okay. Data residency again: suppose you have a burst pool in us-east but it’s “shared” with hosted. Are you mixing government customers with commercial? We have internal segmentation requirements.

[11:16] Marcus Lin: We have separate environments for regulated workloads where required. For the burst beta, eligibility is controlled — we can ensure your burst pools only include tenants of the same compliance tier. We can also commit to not placing you in a pool that includes certain categories.

[11:34] Ariana Patel: That’s important. Can we get that in writing? Like, pool eligibility criteria.

[11:39] Markus Klein: Yes. We’ll add that to the beta terms and the one-pager. There’s a concept of “pool class” internally.

[11:48] Mikhail Orlov: How do you enforce that? Tagging?

[11:52] Ethan Park: Pool labels and policy engine enforcement. The policy engine checks tenant eligibility against pool class before admitting.

[12:03] Ariana Patel: Is that deterministic? Like, we don’t want weird race conditions where it routes incorrectly.

[12:08] Ethan Park: Deterministic and cached. There’s a single evaluation path. We also have audit logs for config changes that affect eligibility.

[12:20] Jonas Meyer: Okay. Another item: do you store any “burst” settings separate from the core tenant config? We need to know where it lives.

[12:29] Ethan Park: It’s part of the tenant config object in the control plane. Same change control, same audit.

[12:37] Ariana Patel: If a Redwood operator needs to disable burst during an incident, does that happen without our approval?

[12:44] Markus Klein: In an incident, yes, we may disable burst to protect your baseline and others. That’s an emergency control and it’s audited. We can also give you an admin API/CLI to disable it yourselves.

[13:01] Sofia Reyes: So you can turn off a feature we paid for?

[13:05] Markus Klein: Only to protect reliability under emergency conditions. And it’s typically temporary. It’s similar to feature flags. We’d document it and communicate.

[13:15] Ariana Patel: From a security perspective, that’s fine, as long as it’s logged.

[13:20] Marcus Lin: It is logged, including the operator identity and the reason ticket link.

[13:28] Mikhail Orlov: Is there any concept of “preemption” in burst? Like we get kicked off mid-stream?

[13:34] Ethan Park: In v1 we favor strict admission control rather than preemption. So once admitted, we try to complete. But under extreme conditions, you could see failures like any shared system; we don’t promise preemption order. We’d rather deny up front than evict later.

[13:56] Ariana Patel: Okay. Another detail: encryption. Is traffic to burst pools encrypted in transit? And at rest? Not sure there is “at rest.”

[14:05] Marcus Lin: In transit yes, TLS. At rest: for any persisted metadata like logs, metrics, audit events, yes encrypted at rest. For in-memory inference, there’s not a storage layer, but we do standard node disk encryption on ephemeral volumes.

[14:22] Jonas Meyer: Customer-managed keys? KMS.

[14:25] Markus Klein: For Dedicated and Private we can do KMS integrations. For this beta, we can keep the same keying model you already have; burst doesn’t change it. If you require CMEK for every log artifact, we’ll confirm region support.

[14:44] Ariana Patel: What about model weights? Are you running the same weights in burst pools, and do you keep them on disk?

[14:51] Kaitlyn Nguyen: Model weights are our assets and are present on nodes. That’s separate from customer data. They’re stored on encrypted volumes; access is restricted.

[15:03] Ariana Patel: Sure. Another angle: are the burst pools in the same VPC as our dedicated environment? We care about network boundaries.

[15:11] Kaitlyn Nguyen: For Dedicated, your baseline is in an isolated tenant network segment. Burst pools are separate; they’re not inside your private segment in the sense of “your VPC.” But the request path still goes through the Redwood control plane and service mesh with tenant auth enforced.

[15:29] Mikhail Orlov: So it’s not like you peer our VPC to that pool.

[15:32] Kaitlyn Nguyen: Correct.

[15:34] Ariana Patel: For some of our policies, “processing outside the dedicated environment” is a flag. But we may allow it with controls. We’ll take this back.

[15:44] Markus Klein: Makes sense. That’s why it’s opt-in and why the guardrails and transparency matter.

[15:52] Jonas Meyer: Transparency: can we see metrics distinguishing baseline vs burst usage?

[15:57] Ethan Park: Yes. We tag usage records as baseline vs burst. In beta it’s shadow metering — not billed yet — but visible.

[16:07] Ariana Patel: And logs? Can we see admission rejects by reason?

[16:11] Ethan Park: Yes, in dashboards and via API. You’ll see “denied due to tenant cap,” “denied due to pool saturation,” “denied due to cooldown,” stuff like that.

[16:25] Mikhail Orlov: Cooldown? Explain.

[16:28] Ethan Park: If a tenant repeatedly hits caps, we apply a backoff window to prevent thrashing the pool. It’s configurable but we have safe defaults.

[16:42] Ariana Patel: That has security implications too — prevents abuse.

[16:45] Marcus Lin: Exactly. It reduces the blast radius.

[16:50] Sofia Reyes: On pricing, you said shadow billing. So we won’t be charged during beta?

[16:55] Markus Klein: Correct. During beta/pilot, we’ll meter it but not invoice; we’ll share reconciliation reports.

[17:05] Jonas Meyer: Back to audit logs: do you also audit policy changes like “pool eligibility class” changes?

[17:12] Ethan Park: Yes. Any config change to your tenant settings is audited. Pool-level changes by Redwood operators are also audited in our internal system; we can provide an attestation if needed, but we don’t expose internal infra changes as customer audit logs today.

[17:32] Ariana Patel: That’s okay. We mainly need customer-scoped audit plus assurance that your operators are controlled.

[17:38] Marcus Lin: We can provide that via SOC 2 and internal access controls. For burst specifically, we can show the new audit event types.

[17:49] Mikhail Orlov: One thing: “shared pool” implies noisy neighbor. You said you don’t do two customers in one process. But do you do MIG? Like splitting a GPU?

[17:59] Kaitlyn Nguyen: Not in this beta. We generally allocate full GPUs to a worker group; we’re not slicing GPUs across tenants.

[18:09] Ariana Patel: That’s good. But if the pool is saturated, can another tenant’s burst traffic push our tail latency up even if admitted?

[18:18] Ethan Park: It can, if overall pool load increases, which is why we have pool-wide saturation gates and fairness. We also monitor tail latency drift and can trip a global circuit breaker to stop bursting.

[18:35] Jonas Meyer: Circuit breaker is automatic? Or manual?

[18:38] Ethan Park: Both. Automatic thresholding on saturation and p99 drift, plus manual kill switch.

[18:45] Ariana Patel: Is that kill switch audited?

[18:47] Ethan Park: Yes.

[18:52] Markus Klein: Ariana, would it help if we separate questions: isolation, audit, residency. I think we’re mostly through isolation and residency.

[18:59] Ariana Patel: Yeah, I have one more isolation question: can burst ever run in a different “compliance tier” environment? Like a lower-tier region?

[19:08] Kaitlyn Nguyen: No. Eligibility is constrained by compliance tier and region. If you’re in a dedicated enterprise tier, you don’t burst into a lower tier pool.

[19:18] Ariana Patel: Okay. For data residency, can you confirm you don’t do any cross-border routing? Like EU to US.

[19:25] Markus Klein: Correct. If your tenant is EU, burst pools are EU only. For Northpeak you’re US-based, but same idea.

[19:33] Mikhail Orlov: What about control plane metadata? Does it live in a single region?

[19:39] Marcus Lin: Control plane is multi-region. Customer content isn’t stored there. Audit logs and metadata can be region-scoped depending on your setup. We’ll align with your requirements.

[19:55] Jonas Meyer: We will likely require audit logs to remain in US regions.

[19:59] Markus Klein: Noted. We can support that.

[20:03] Ariana Patel: Okay, now audit log details. You said diff summary. Is it machine-readable JSON? We need to parse.

[20:10] Ethan Park: Yes, it’s structured. For customers we typically provide a JSON schema. I’ll send a sample event payload (redacted).

[20:21] Ariana Patel: Great. Include fields like old_value/new_value, actor_id, actor_email, source_ip.

[20:27] Ethan Park: Yep.

[20:29] Sofia Reyes: One question: who signs the beta terms? We need to ensure security addendum includes this.

[20:35] Markus Klein: We’ll route through our standard order form addendum; legal will attach. For beta, it’s typically a pilot agreement.

[20:44] Ariana Patel: We also want a statement that payload logging is off by default, and if enabled, it’s customer-controlled.

[20:52] Marcus Lin: We can include that.

[20:56] Mikhail Orlov: Operationally, can we see when a request was served via burst vs baseline? Like header or log field.

[21:03] Ethan Park: There’s a response header indicating burst admission, and a trace attribute if you use our tracing integration.

[21:12] Ariana Patel: Does that header leak information? Like pool id.

[21:16] Ethan Park: We don’t include internal pool IDs. It’s a boolean and a reason code if denied.

[21:24] Jonas Meyer: That helps for incident forensics.

[21:27] Markus Klein: Exactly.

[21:31] Ariana Patel: Last thing: if burst is enabled, can Redwood use it to migrate us off dedicated capacity more generally? Like, would you reduce our baseline?

[21:41] Markus Klein: No. Baseline Dedicated capacity remains as contracted. Burst is additive and best-effort within caps. It’s not a way for us to dilute your reserved capacity.

[21:53] Mikhail Orlov: And “best-effort” meaning no SLA for burst latency?

[21:58] Markus Klein: Right now, burst has operational targets but not the same SLA as baseline. That’s part of why we’re doing pilot/beta.

[22:08] Ariana Patel: Okay. I think we’re good. Can you recap what you’re sending?

[22:13] Markus Klein: Yup. We’ll send: (1) burst pool topology + region pinning doc, (2) sample audit log events for burst config changes, (3) note on isolation model — no multi-tenant in same inference process — and (4) options for SIEM export.

[22:31] Jonas Meyer: And maybe confirm whether any data crosses regions in control plane.

[22:35] Marcus Lin: We’ll add a written clarification.

[22:38] Ariana Patel: Great.

[22:41] Markus Klein: Anything else from your side?

[22:44] Sofia Reyes: Just timeline. When do you need a decision?

[22:48] Markus Klein: For the pilot slot, next two weeks. But security approval can proceed in parallel. We can schedule a follow-up once you review the docs.

[23:00] Ariana Patel: Sounds good.

[23:02] (cross talk / audio)

[23:05] Markus Klein: Cool, thanks all. We’ll follow up via email.

---

Note: Transcript continues with light scheduling chatter until end of recording; no additional substantive security content.

[46:58] Recording ended.
